task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-05-23, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
If PNR fail then PULL_UP is a real league-wide counter, it should show lift>0 in >=70% of units with median lift>2pp.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: lift threshold (positive in ≥70% of units, median >2 pp100)
methodological_questions: Operational definition of 'PNR fail': is it the project's suppression trigger (within-game H1-to-H2 PPP drop with minimum attempts)?
Unit of analysis: what constitutes a 'unit' (team-season, team-defense pairing, game, matchup)?
Measurement of lift: baseline for expected pull-up PPP (team's own non-trigger pull-up efficiency, league average, or expected points model)?
Timing of counter: are pull-up possessions counted only in the same game after the trigger, or in subsequent games?
Minimum sample size: how many trigger events and pull-up possessions does each unit need to estimate lift reliably?
Threshold criteria: statistical test for '≥70% of units' and 'median lift >2 pp100' jointly, accounting for estimation uncertainty?
Reliability of play-type classification for PNR and PULL_UP, especially from the inferrer.
Sparsity: how many suppression triggers occur per team per season, and how many pull-up possessions follow?
evidence_establishes: No previous study families were retrieved, so no conclusions can be drawn from earlier work.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether pull-up jumpers are an effective counter after PNR failure, at any threshold.
Whether the proposed 70%/2pp rule has been tested or is a reasonable expectation.
own_inferences: The question likely uses the project's suppression-trigger framework: a game where PNR PPP falls from H1 to H2 under minimum-attempt rules.
The natural unit is a team-season (offense), giving ~120 units across the four available seasons.
Each team-season will have only a modest number of trigger games (probably <10), and only a subset of possessions after the trigger will be pull-ups; this makes lift estimates noisy.
A lift metric needs a carefully chosen baseline (e.g., same team's pull-up PPP in non-trigger games matched by opponent strength and game situation) to avoid confounding.
The joint threshold (≥70% of units with lift>0 and median lift>2 pp100) is a strong claim that may be hard to meet even if a real effect exists, unless the effect is large and consistent.

Regression to the mean may inflate apparent lift because triggers are defined by an extreme drop in PNR efficiency, which could be partly random; however, pull-ups are a different play type, so RTM may be limited.
uncertainties: The exact empirical distribution of suppression triggers on PNR across the league is unknown; the number of trigger games per team-season could be very low, threatening feasibility.
The quality of the play-type classification for pull-up jumpers (especially from play-by-play text) is not quantified; misclassification could dilute or bias the lift estimates.
There is no agreed-upon baseline for pull-up PPP; using a naive comparison (e.g., league average) could create a mechanical floor effect.
Game-strategy confounding: after a PNR is taken away, the offense may be forced into more difficult pull-up attempts late in the shot clock, which could mask or reverse a true counter effect.
Coaching adjustments and personnel substitutions after a trigger may confound the observed lift, making it unclear whether the pull-up itself is effective or the overall adjusted game plan.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieval returned no records, so the decision is based entirely on a conceptual and methodological assessment of the question and data.

blocking_constraints.text: Suppression triggers on PNR are likely rare; many team-seasons may have fewer than 5 triggers, providing too few pull-up possessions to estimate lift reliably per unit.

Even with ~120 team-seasons, the small number of trigger games per unit may yield low statistical power to detect whether ≥70% of units have positive lift, especially after accounting for estimation uncertainty.
The project's play-type classifier (including the inferrer) may mislabel possessions, especially distinguishing pull-up jumpers from other off-dribble shots; this adds noise and potential bias.

prior_work.summary: No earlier study families were returned, so it is unknown whether similar questions have been tested before.

risks.text: Very few PNR suppression triggers per team-season and even fewer subsequent pull-up possessions; aggregated per-unit lift estimates may be dominated by a handful of events.
Low effective sample size per unit reduces power to correctly classify units as having positive or negative lift, and to estimate the median lift with precision.
Play-type labels (PNR, PULL_UP) may contain systematic error, especially from the inferrer step; validation studies are needed.
Observed pull-up PPP after a trigger may reflect opponent defensive adjustments, score effects, shot-clock pressure, and personnel changes, not solely the counter strategy.
Selecting games by extreme H1-to-H2 PNR PPP drops may induce regression to the mean in subsequent possessions, although it may be partially mitigated by changing play type.
Lift is derived from observed PPP; the choice of baseline (e.g., team average, expected points model) can create an illusion of effectiveness if not properly counterfactual.
If the suppression trigger is defined using full-game data, the counter could be contaminated by lookahead; must limit trigger detection to H1 only.
Testing across many units and possibly across multiple counter play types inflates family-wise error if not corrected; the stated joint threshold partially addresses this.
Complex pipeline from play-by-play to play-type classification to suppression triggers and lift computation introduces many potential coding errors.
Playing style and pull-up efficiency may drift over the four seasons; pooling across seasons could violate stationarity assumptions.

design.estimand: Causal lift of pull-up jumper efficiency (points per 100 possessions) immediately after a defensive suppression trigger on pick-and-roll ball-handler possessions, relative to the same team's pull-up efficiency in comparable non-trigger games.
design.unit: Team-season (offensive team across a full NBA season, including playoffs).
design.sample: All team-seasons from 2022-23 through 2025-26 with at least one valid PNR suppression trigger, using possession-level data from the project's graph database, excluding garbage time (score margin ≥25 in second half) and transition possessions.
design.power: Pilot simulation using the actual distribution of trigger counts per team-season from the data. Minimum target: 80% probability that a true median lift of 3 pp100 and true proportion >0.80 yields a posterior probability >0.95 that the decision rule is met, assuming shrinkage priors. If pilot shows insufficient power, pool multiple seasons or redefine unit as team (all seasons combined).
design.controls: Fixed effects: opponent defensive rating (rolling 20-game average), home/away, rest days, game quarter (1st/2nd half after trigger), score margin at time of possession, possession shot-clock remaining, and presence of the team's primary initiator. Random intercepts: team-season and opponent.
design.falsification: 1. Test lift for pull-up possessions in the first half of the same game (before the trigger is established) — should be near zero. 2. Replace PNR suppression trigger with a placebo trigger on a play type that is not expected to produce a pull-up counter (e.g., PUTBACK) and test for lift. 3. Test lift for a different counter play type (e.g., post-up) where no hypothesis is made.
design.multiplicity: Primary test is a single joint decision: posterior probability that (proportion of units with positive lift) > 0.70 AND median lift > 2 pp100 exceeds 0.95. No separate per-unit tests are reported as confirmatory. All other analyses (subgroups, seasons, etc.) are exploratory.
design.decision_rule: Estimate the posterior distribution of (proportion positive, median lift) using a Bayesian hierarchical model (beta-binomial for unit-level sign, Gaussian for lift with team-season random effects). Conclude supported if P(proportion >0.70 and median >2) > 0.95; reject if P(either condition fails) > 0.95; otherwise uncertain. Prior distributions chosen via predictive checking on placebo data.
design.data_version: Play-by-play and derived possession data from the NBA stats API, frozen as of 2026-06-21. All play-type classifications from the project's graph database, using the rule-based classifier (including inferrer) with version tag noted.
